title: Datasets Library
description: Load and explore Hub datasets, transform them at scale with map() and filter(), build clean train/val/test splits, and understand what data collators do at batch time.

lessons.title: Loading and Exploring a Dataset
lessons.description: Load a dataset from the Hub and inspect it like the DataFrame exploration you did in the data science course.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can load a dataset from the Hub with the `datasets` library and inspect its structure.

sections.title: 📦 A DataFrame-like object, built for ML
sections.content:
The `datasets` library's `load_dataset()` downloads a dataset from the Hub and returns a `Dataset` object (or `DatasetDict` with named splits like `train`/`test`). It behaves a bit like the pandas DataFrames from the data science course, but is built for memory-efficient, large-scale ML workflows.

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset("imdb")
print(dataset)
# DatasetDict({'train': Dataset(...), 'test': Dataset(...), ...})

print(dataset["train"][0])
# {'text': 'This movie was...', 'label': 0}
```

sections.title: 🔍 Inspecting before you train
sections.content:
Just like the EDA lesson in the data science course, always look at raw examples, class balance, and text length distribution before fine-tuning anything on a new dataset — the same 'know your data first' principle applies here.

```python
print(dataset["train"].features)   # column names & types
print(len(dataset["train"]))       # number of examples
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Fine-tuning without checking class balance.** A dataset that's 95% one label will bias your model unless you account for it.

**Assuming the Hub's preset splits are always ideal for your task.** Sometimes you need to re-split or combine splits yourself.

**Not checking text length distribution before setting `max_length`.** If most examples are short but a few are very long, your truncation strategy should reflect that.

questions.question: What does `load_dataset("imdb")` return?
options: A single Python list with no structure
A DatasetDict (or Dataset) object containing the data, typically organized into named splits like train and test
A trained model ready for inference
A raw CSV file only, no parsing
questions.explanation: load_dataset returns a structured object — usually a DatasetDict with named splits (train, test, etc.), each holding a Dataset you can index, inspect, and transform.

questions.question: Why should you inspect class balance before fine-tuning on a dataset?
options: Class balance never affects model training
A dataset dominated by one label can bias the model toward that label unless you account for the imbalance
Class balance only matters for image data
Datasets are always perfectly balanced by default
questions.explanation: Just as in the data science course's discussion of imbalanced data, a model fine-tuned on a heavily skewed dataset will tend to over-predict the majority class unless the imbalance is addressed.

questions.question: Why is checking text length distribution useful before setting a tokenizer's `max_length`?
options: Text length has no relationship to tokenization settings
If most examples are short but a few are very long, your truncation strategy should reflect that instead of blindly picking one fixed length
max_length is set automatically and cannot be changed
Text length only matters for image datasets
questions.explanation: Knowing the length distribution tells you whether a chosen max_length will truncate a small handful of outliers or a large chunk of your data — exactly the kind of exploratory check the data science course taught before any modeling decision.

questions.question: What does `load_dataset("imdb")` typically return?
options: A single unstructured Python list

A trained model ready for immediate inference

questions.explanation: load_dataset returns a structured object, usually a DatasetDict with named splits (like train and test), each holding a Dataset you can index, inspect, and transform.

lessons.title: Transforming Data with map() and filter()
lessons.description: Apply a function across an entire dataset efficiently, including tokenization at scale.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can use `.map()` to apply a transformation (like tokenization) across a whole dataset.

sections.title: 🗺️ map() applies a function to every example
🚀 batched=True for speed
sections.content: Setting `batched=True` passes a batch of examples to your function at once instead of one row at a time, which lets the fast tokenizer batch its own work internally — often a large speedup for tokenization specifically.

sections.title: 🧹 filter() removes rows you don't want
sections.content:
`.filter()` keeps only the rows where a function returns `True` — useful for removing empty texts, out-of-range labels, or examples that are too long before training even starts.

```python
cleaned = dataset.filter(lambda ex: len(ex["text"]) > 0)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Forgetting `batched=True` for tokenization.** Row-by-row tokenization works but is much slower than letting the fast tokenizer batch internally.

**Mutating a dataset in place expecting the original to change.** `.map()` and `.filter()` return new datasets — you need to assign the result.

**Filtering after tokenizing instead of before.** Filtering first (e.g. removing empty texts) avoids wasting compute tokenizing rows you'll throw away anyway.

questions.question: What does `dataset.map(tokenize_fn, batched=True)` do?
options: Deletes the dataset
Applies tokenize_fn across the dataset, passing batches of examples at a time, and returns a new dataset with the results
Trains a model directly on the dataset
Only works on datasets with fewer than 100 rows
questions.explanation: map() runs the given function across the dataset (in batches, when batched=True) and returns a new dataset containing the transformed results — commonly used to tokenize an entire dataset at once.

questions.question: Why does setting `batched=True` typically speed up tokenization with `.map()`?
options: It doesn't speed anything up, it's purely stylistic
It lets the fast tokenizer process many examples together internally, which is much more efficient than tokenizing one row at a time
batched=True skips tokenization entirely
It only affects how the results are printed
questions.explanation: Fast tokenizers are optimized for batch processing. Passing a batch of examples at once (batched=True) lets that internal batching kick in, which is usually significantly faster than one row at a time.

questions.question: Why is it usually better to filter out unwanted rows (like empty texts) before tokenizing rather than after?
options: Order never matters for map/filter operations
Filtering first avoids spending compute tokenizing rows that will just be discarded afterward anyway
You cannot filter after tokenizing, only before
Filtering after tokenizing produces different, more accurate results
questions.explanation: Since tokenization takes compute time, removing rows you don't want (like empty strings) before tokenizing means you never waste that work on data you were going to throw away regardless.

questions.question: What does `dataset.map(tokenize_fn, batched=True)` do?
options: It permanently deletes the dataset
It applies tokenize_fn across the dataset, passing batches of examples at a time, and returns a new dataset with the results
It trains a model directly using the dataset
It only works if the dataset has fewer than 100 rows
questions.explanation: map() runs the given function across the dataset (in batches when batched=True) and returns a new dataset containing the transformed results, commonly used for tokenizing an entire dataset at once.

questions.question: What earlier data science course concept does `.map()` resemble, according to this lesson?
options: The train/test split function
The `.apply()` method on a pandas Series, but built to handle datasets far larger than memory
A confusion matrix
A correlation heatmap
questions.explanation: The lesson describes .map() as the ML equivalent of pandas' .apply() method from the data science course, adapted to handle datasets far larger than memory.

questions.question: Why does setting `batched=True` typically speed up tokenization with `.map()`?
options: It doesn't speed anything up; it's purely stylistic
It lets the fast tokenizer process many examples together internally, which is much more efficient than tokenizing one row at a time
batched=True skips tokenization entirely
It only changes how results are displayed, not computed
questions.explanation: Fast tokenizers are optimized for batch processing, so passing a batch of examples at once lets that internal batching kick in, usually producing a significant speedup over row-by-row tokenization.

questions.question: What does `.filter()` do to a dataset?
options: It deletes the entire dataset
It keeps only the rows where a given function returns True
It trains a model on the filtered rows automatically
It renames the dataset's columns
questions.explanation: .filter() keeps only the rows where the provided function returns True, useful for removing empty texts, out-of-range labels, or overly long examples before training even starts.

questions.question: Why is it usually better to filter out unwanted rows before tokenizing rather than after?
options: Order never matters for map/filter operations
Filtering first avoids spending compute tokenizing rows that will just be discarded afterward anyway
You cannot filter a dataset after tokenizing it, only before
Filtering after tokenizing always produces more accurate results
questions.explanation: Since tokenization takes compute time, removing unwanted rows (like empty strings) before tokenizing means that compute is never wasted on data that would be thrown away regardless.

lessons.title: Train/Validation/Test Splits Done Right
lessons.description: Apply the train/val/test discipline from the ML course to Hugging Face datasets specifically.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can create clean train/validation/test splits from a Hugging Face dataset, avoiding leakage.

sections.title: 🔁 The same discipline, a new library
sections.content:
The machine learning course covered why train/validation/test splits (and avoiding leakage) matter. The `datasets` library gives you `.train_test_split()` to do this cleanly, including stratifying by label to preserve class balance across splits.

```python
split = dataset["train"].train_test_split(test_size=0.2, seed=42, stratify_by_column="label")
train_ds, val_ds = split["train"], split["test"]
```

sections.title: 🚫 Watching for leakage in text data
sections.content: Leakage in text datasets often looks different from tabular leakage: duplicate or near-duplicate examples across splits (e.g. the same review appearing twice with slightly different wording) can silently inflate validation accuracy. Deduplicate before splitting when this is a risk.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Not setting a `seed`.** Without a fixed seed, your split changes every run, making experiments impossible to reproduce.

**Forgetting `stratify_by_column` on imbalanced data.** A random split can accidentally starve one split of minority-class examples.

**Reusing the test set to tune hyperparameters.** Exactly the ML course's warning — the test set should only be touched once, at the very end.

questions.question: Why does `train_test_split(seed=42, ...)` matter for reproducibility?
options: The seed value has no effect on the split
Without a fixed seed, the random split changes every time the code runs, making experiments impossible to reproduce exactly
seed only affects the model, not the dataset
Seeds are required by the Hugging Face terms of service
questions.explanation: Setting a seed makes the 'random' split deterministic — running the same code again produces the exact same train/validation split, which is essential for reproducible experiments.

questions.question: Why would you use `stratify_by_column="label"` when splitting an imbalanced dataset?
options: It has no effect on class distribution
Without it, a random split could accidentally leave one split with very few examples of a minority class, distorting evaluation
Stratification is only relevant for numeric labels, never categorical ones
It automatically balances the dataset by duplicating minority examples
questions.explanation: Stratifying preserves each split's class proportions to match the original dataset, preventing a random split from accidentally starving the validation or test set of minority-class examples.

questions.question: Why can duplicate or near-duplicate examples across train and validation splits be a leakage problem specific to text data?
options: Duplicates never cause any issues in text data
A model can effectively memorize a near-duplicate example seen in training, inflating validation performance in a way that doesn't reflect real generalization
Text datasets cannot contain duplicates by design
This is only a concern for image datasets, not text
questions.explanation: If a near-duplicate of a training example ends up in validation, the model may 'recognize' it rather than generalize to it, making validation accuracy look better than the model's true performance on genuinely new data.

questions.question: What earlier course's discipline does this lesson apply specifically to Hugging Face datasets?
options: The data science course's visualization lessons
The machine learning course's guidance on train/validation/test splits and avoiding leakage
The NLP course's tokenization lessons
The computer vision course's augmentation lessons
questions.explanation: This lesson applies the machine learning course's train/validation/test split discipline, including avoiding leakage, specifically using the datasets library's tools.

questions.question: Why does `train_test_split(seed=42, ...)` matter for reproducibility?
options: The seed value has no actual effect on the split
Without a fixed seed, the random split changes every run, making experiments impossible to reproduce exactly
seed only affects the model architecture, not the dataset
Seeds are required by Hugging Face's terms of service
questions.explanation: Setting a seed makes the random split deterministic, so running the same code again produces the exact same train/validation split — essential for reproducible experiments.

questions.question: Why would you use `stratify_by_column="label"` when splitting an imbalanced dataset?
options: It has no effect on the resulting class distribution
Without it, a random split could accidentally leave one split with very few examples of a minority class, distorting evaluation
Stratification only works with numeric labels, never categorical ones
It automatically duplicates minority-class examples to balance the dataset
questions.explanation: Stratifying preserves each split's class proportions to match the original dataset, preventing a random split from accidentally starving the validation or test set of minority-class examples.

questions.question: How does leakage in text datasets often look different from leakage in tabular data, according to this lesson?
options: Text data can never experience any form of leakage
Duplicate or near-duplicate examples across splits (like the same review reworded slightly) can silently inflate validation accuracy
Leakage in text data always inflates loss rather than accuracy
Text and tabular leakage look identical in every respect
questions.explanation: The lesson highlights that text-specific leakage often takes the form of duplicate or near-duplicate examples appearing across splits, which can silently inflate validation performance.

questions.question: What warning from the machine learning course does this lesson repeat regarding the test set?
options: The test set should be used to tune hyperparameters repeatedly
The test set should only be touched once, at the very end, not reused to tune hyperparameters
There is no meaningful difference between validation and test sets
Test sets are unnecessary once you have a validation set
questions.explanation: The lesson repeats the machine learning course's warning that reusing the test set to tune hyperparameters defeats its purpose — it should be touched only once, at the very end.

lessons.title: Data Collators and Dynamic Padding
lessons.description: Understand what a data collator does and why dynamic padding saves compute.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what a data collator does and why dynamic padding is more efficient than fixed padding.

sections.title: 🧱 Assembling a batch at the last moment
sections.content:
A **data collator** takes a list of individual examples and assembles them into a single batch, applying padding at that point rather than ahead of time. `DataCollatorWithPadding` pads each batch only to the length of its own longest sequence.

```python
from transformers import DataCollatorWithPadding

collator = DataCollatorWithPadding(tokenizer=tokenizer)
batch = collator([tokenized[0], tokenized[1], tokenized[2]])
```

sections.title: ⚡ Dynamic padding saves real compute
sections.content: If you padded every example to the model's absolute maximum length ahead of time, most batches would be full of wasted `[PAD]` tokens. Padding **dynamically**, per batch, at collation time means a batch of naturally short sentences stays short, and only a batch that happens to contain a long sentence pays that cost.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Pre-padding the whole dataset to max_length.** This works but wastes memory and compute compared to per-batch dynamic padding.

**Using the wrong collator for the task.** Classification, token classification (NER), and language modeling each have their own collator that handles labels differently — using a mismatched one silently breaks label alignment.

**Forgetting the collator needs the same tokenizer as the model.** Padding uses the tokenizer's pad token id, which must match what the model expects.

questions.question: What does a data collator like `DataCollatorWithPadding` do?
options: It trains the model
It assembles a list of individual examples into a batch, applying padding at that point based on the batch's own longest sequence
It deletes examples that are too long
It tokenizes raw text for the first time
questions.explanation: The collator's job is batch assembly: given individual tokenized examples, it pads them to a common length (the batch's own maximum) and stacks them into tensors ready for the model.

questions.question: Why is dynamic (per-batch) padding more efficient than padding every example to the model's absolute maximum length ahead of time?
options: There is no efficiency difference between the two approaches
Pre-padding to the absolute maximum wastes compute on [PAD] tokens even in batches where every real sequence is short
Dynamic padding is always less accurate
Dynamic padding is only usable during inference, never training
questions.explanation: With dynamic padding, each batch is only padded to its own longest sequence. A batch of short sentences stays short and cheap to process, instead of being padded out to the model's overall maximum length regardless of actual content.

questions.question: Why does a task like token classification (NER) need a different data collator than plain text classification?
options: It doesn't — every task uses the exact same collator
Token classification has per-token labels that need to be padded and aligned consistently with the padded input tokens, which a plain classification collator doesn't handle
NER never uses batching at all
Collators are unrelated to the type of task being trained
questions.explanation: Token classification labels one entry per input token, so padding the inputs also requires padding the labels in a matching, aligned way — something a plain sequence-classification collator (with one label per example) isn't built to do.

questions.question: What does a data collator like `DataCollatorWithPadding` do?
options: It trains the model directly
It assembles a list of individual examples into a batch, applying padding based on that batch's own longest sequence
It permanently deletes examples that are too long
It performs the very first tokenization of raw text
questions.explanation: A collator's job is batch assembly: given individually tokenized examples, it pads them to a common length (the batch's own maximum) and stacks them into tensors ready for the model.

questions.question: Why is dynamic (per-batch) padding more efficient than pre-padding every example to the model's absolute maximum length?
options: There is no efficiency difference between the two approaches
Pre-padding to the absolute maximum wastes compute on [PAD] tokens even in batches where every real sequence is short
Dynamic padding is always less accurate than pre-padding
Dynamic padding can only be used during inference, never training
questions.explanation: With dynamic padding, each batch is only padded to its own longest sequence, so a batch of naturally short sentences stays cheap to process instead of being padded to the model's overall maximum regardless of actual content.

questions.question: Why does token classification (like NER) need a different data collator than plain text classification?
options: It doesn't — every task uses the exact same collator
Token classification has per-token labels that need to be padded and aligned with the padded inputs, which a plain classification collator doesn't handle
NER tasks never use batching of any kind
Collators have no relationship to the specific task being trained
questions.explanation: Since token classification assigns one label per input token, padding the inputs also requires padding the labels in an aligned way — something a plain sequence-classification collator, built for one label per example, isn't designed to do.

questions.question: Why must a data collator use the same tokenizer as the model it's feeding?
options: The collator's tokenizer choice has no effect on anything
Padding uses the tokenizer's pad token id, which must match what the model expects
Collators never actually interact with tokenizers at all
Any tokenizer can be used interchangeably with any collator and model combination
questions.explanation: The collator pads using the tokenizer's specific pad token id — if this doesn't match what the model expects, the padding could be misinterpreted, so the collator must use the same tokenizer as the model.

questions.question: What is the main downside of pre-padding the entire dataset to `max_length` ahead of time, rather than using a collator's dynamic padding?
options: There is no downside; the two approaches are functionally identical
It wastes memory and compute compared to per-batch dynamic padding
Pre-padding always produces incorrect model outputs
Pre-padding is not technically possible with Hugging Face tools
questions.explanation: Pre-padding every example to the model's absolute maximum length ahead of time works, but wastes memory and compute compared to padding dynamically per batch at collation time.
